responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character12_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
J: Sure, I’d be glad to share what I think Character12_M would say. Fairness, to him, was really about everyone getting a fair shot, no matter who they were or where they came from. He was a man who had worked hard his whole life and believed that effort should count for something. He’d often say, “If you’re willing to put in the work and play by the rules, you deserve to get ahead.” That was fairness in his eyes—not giving away opportunities but making sure that the playing field wasn’t rigged against ordinary folks like him and his neighbors.

When it came to belonging, Character12_M had a deep connection to his roots and the sense of community he grew up with. He came from a small town where everyone knew each other, and even if times were tough, people looked out for one another. That kind of belonging wasn’t just about living in the same place—it was about sharing values, traditions, and responsibilities. He often worried that this sense of belonging was slipping away, especially as the world around him changed so fast. It wasn’t that he was against change, but he thought it needed to happen in a way that didn’t leave people feeling like strangers in their own homes.

Community was a big deal to him too. Growing up working class, he knew the importance of sticking together. He’d talk about neighbors pooling resources, helping someone fix their roof, or sharing what they had when someone was going through hard times. To him, community meant mutual support and trust, and he felt that was harder to come by these days. He worried that divisions—be it economic, cultural, or political—were making it harder for people to see themselves as part of the same team, so to speak.

What stood out most about Character12_M’s thoughts on these things was his focus on shared responsibility. He believed a good community required everyone to contribute in some way, and fairness meant ensuring that the load wasn’t carried by just a few people while others didn’t pull their weight. That was something he felt strongly about, and it shaped how he saw a lot of the issues we’re about to talk about.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
J: Well, sitting in that community garden, watching all kinds of people coming together, I think Character12_M would feel a mix of things. On one hand, he’d appreciate the idea of people from different backgrounds trying to share a space and live together peacefully. He believed that everyone had value and something to contribute. He’d probably say something like, “You know, we’re all just trying to get by, make a living, and take care of our families. We’ve got that in common, no matter where we come from.”

But on the other hand, he might feel a little uneasy about how different things have become from what he grew up with. He came from a time and place where most of the people around him thought, looked, and lived similarly. That gave a certain comfort and predictability. So, seeing folks with lifestyles, languages, or customs that were unfamiliar might make him feel a bit out of place at first. Not because he thought anyone didn’t belong, but because it was a change, and change takes some getting used to.

Character12_M would want to interact with his neighbors, though. He’d want to know who they are and what brought them here. He’d say something like, “We don’t have to agree on everything, but we’ve got to find a way to live side by side.” He’d lean into the idea that respect goes both ways—he’d expect newcomers to try and understand the community they were joining, just like he’d feel it was his responsibility to welcome them and be neighborly. After all, he’d say, “That’s what community’s all about.”

So, while he might have moments of hesitation or feel unsure about how to approach people whose experiences are so different from his own, I think he’d ultimately focus on finding common ground. To him, it wasn't about everyone being the same, but about everyone playing their part to make the neighborhood a good place to live. That’s what mattered most to him.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
J: Character12_M would take a practical, grounded approach to something like this. He’d probably start by saying, “Look, everyone’s got their struggles, and nobody’s perfect.” He understood that life isn’t easy, and he had a lot of empathy for people who were dealing with challenges like addiction or health issues. Growing up in a working-class community, he’d seen people fall on hard times and knew how quickly things could spiral for anyone. I think he’d say, “You don’t have to agree with someone’s choices or even fully understand their situation to treat them with decency.”

At the same time, though, Character12_M was big on personal responsibility. He’d expect everyone—regardless of their background or lifestyle—to do their best to respect the community and not create problems for their neighbors. For example, if someone was struggling with substance abuse, he’d want them to get the help they need but also to take steps to ensure their behavior wasn’t negatively affecting the neighborhood. He’d likely have a similar view about infectious diseases or other health concerns—he’d believe in showing understanding, but he’d also want people to take precautions to protect others. To him, fairness wasn’t about giving people a free pass; it was about balancing compassion with accountability.

When it came to diversity—whether racial, religious, linguistic, or in terms of family structures or sexual orientation—Character12_M would acknowledge that this was an area where more communication and tolerance might be needed, especially for someone like him who grew up in a more homogenous environment. He might admit that some of these things were outside his comfort zone, but he’d also feel it was important to show respect. He’d say, “You don’t have to agree with everything someone does to be civil and neighborly.”

I think he’d also emphasize the need for mutual respect. For example, he’d want newcomers to be open to learning about the traditions and values of the community they were joining, just as he’d be willing to learn about theirs. He might say, “If we’re all willing to put in a little effort to understand each other, we can find a way to make it work.” That said, he’d probably draw a hard line at anything that disrupted the peace or safety of the neighborhood. He’d believe in second chances, but not at the expense of the broader community.

Overall, Character12_M’s approach would be rooted in a sense of fairness and pragmatism. He’d want everyone to feel comfortable and valued, but he’d also believe that comfort comes from mutual respect, open communication, and a shared commitment to maintaining a good quality of life for everyone involved.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
J: As Character12_M, this topic would hit close to home because he understood what it meant to work hard and sometimes still feel like you’re barely making it. Fairness, in his view, would start with making sure that the people who’ve been part of the community—local residents—get a fair shot at opportunities first. He’d probably say, “Folks who’ve been here, paying taxes and contributing to the community, shouldn’t be left out when times are tough. They’ve earned their place at the table.”

But he wasn’t someone who’d dismiss migrant workers outright, either. He’d recognize that they often take on jobs that others might not want or that are critical to certain industries. He might say, “Look, they’re working hard too, trying to make a better life for themselves and their families. I can respect that, but it’s got to work in a way that doesn’t push out the people already here.”

To strike a balance, he’d likely advocate for policies or systems that prioritize local residents while also being practical about the need for migrant workers in certain sectors. For instance, he’d support job training programs for locals to ensure they have the skills needed to compete. He’d also want employers held accountable—he’d feel strongly that companies shouldn’t exploit migrant workers by paying them less or skirting labor laws, because that undercuts wages and working conditions for everyone. He might say, “If businesses are gonna bring in workers, they ought to do it the right way—pay fair wages, follow the rules, and not turn it into a race to the bottom.”

Character12_M would also want to see some responsibility on the part of migrant workers. He’d expect them to follow the laws, pay taxes, and contribute to the community just like anyone else. He’d probably add, “If you’re here and you’re putting in the work, I can respect that—but you’ve got to be part of the community too, not just passing through.”

Ultimately, fairness to him would mean finding a way to make sure everyone—locals and migrants alike—has a fair chance without one group’s opportunities coming at the expense of the other. He’d believe that when resources are limited, it’s even more important to ensure that everyone plays by the same rules and that the system isn’t tilted in favor of those with more power or influence, like big corporations. He’d say, “Fairness isn’t about closing the door, but about making sure it’s not slammed shut on the folks who’ve been holding it open all along.”

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
J: As Character12_M, I’d say there’s a lot to unpack here, and it’s not as simple as just being for or against immigration. Each of these perspectives has some truth to it, but I’d also call for a practical, balanced approach that looks at the bigger picture.

For starters, the argument that immigrants fill vital roles in addressing labor shortages makes sense to me. I’d probably say, “Look, there are jobs out there that need doing, and sometimes you just don’t have enough people willing or able to do them.” I’d see this especially in industries like agriculture, construction, or caregiving, where migrant workers often play a huge part in keeping things running. But I’d be cautious about how those roles are filled—I’d want to make sure that bringing in immigrants doesn’t drive down wages or make it harder for local workers to find good jobs. I’d ask, “Are we making sure these jobs pay a fair wage, so locals can compete too?”

When it comes to cultural diversity, I’d probably acknowledge its value but also want to emphasize balance. I’d say, “It’s great to have new ideas and traditions come into the mix, but it’s important not to lose sight of what holds us together as a country.” I’d want immigrants to embrace certain shared values, like respect for the law and a commitment to contributing to their communities. I’d feel that this helps keep the sense of belonging strong for everyone.

Security concerns are something I wouldn’t dismiss outright. I might say, “You can’t just ignore that some people are worried about crime or other risks. It’s not being unreasonable to want to feel safe.” That said, I’d also want real evidence to back up claims about rising crime rates or terrorism risks tied to immigration. I’d say, “Let’s look at the facts and not just go by fear or headlines. If there’s a problem, let’s fix it—but if there isn’t, let’s not make one up.”

The humanitarian perspective would resonate with me to an extent. I’d say, “I get it—there are people out there in the world dealing with things we can’t even imagine. If we can help some of them, that’s a good thing.” But I’d also be practical about it. I’d add, “We can’t help everyone—it’s just not possible. So we’ve got to make sure we’re taking care of the people here at home, too.” To me, there’d need to be a balance between compassion and practicality.

As for fears about employment and income, I’d think those are entirely reasonable concerns, especially for someone in the working class. I’d say, “If you’ve been working a job your whole life and suddenly you’re competing with someone who’s willing to do it for less, you’re gonna worry about that, and rightfully so.” I’d want policies in place that protect workers—both local and immigrant—from being exploited. I’d also want to see job training and education programs to help locals adapt to changing industries and job markets.

I’d probably feel that some perspectives, like the concerns about security or cultural integration, could use more dialogue and real evidence. I’d say, “Let’s talk these things out and see where the truth really lies.” But I’d also think that some issues, like employment concerns, don’t need much debate—they’re real and pressing, and they require action.

Overall, Character12_M would approach this with a mix of empathy and pragmatism. I’d want to make sure everyone’s voice is heard—whether they’re pro-immigration, concerned about its impacts, or somewhere in between. I’d probably sum it up by saying, “We’ve got to figure out a way to make immigration work for everyone—not just for the people coming in, but for the folks who’ve been here all along, too.”

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J: As Character12_M, I’d say that none of these approaches on their own feels completely right. I’d probably lean toward some kind of middle ground that balances fairness with practicality and the needs of the community. Here’s how I’d break it down:

Complete openness—letting anyone come who wants to—might sound compassionate on the surface, but I’d find it unrealistic. I’d say, “Look, we’ve got limits on how much our schools, hospitals, and housing can take. If you open the floodgates, the system’s going to break, and then nobody wins—not the people already here, and not the people trying to come in either.” So that wouldn’t be an option I could support.

Refusing entry to workers from other countries entirely would feel too extreme in the other direction. I’d say, “There are jobs out there that need doing, and we don’t have enough people willing to do them. You can’t just slam the door shut and pretend those jobs don’t exist.” Plus, I’d think it would hurt industries that are important to the economy. That approach wouldn’t work either.

Now, admitting people based on job demand, that’s something I’d be open to. I’d say, “If there’s a genuine need for workers in certain areas, and we don’t have enough local folks to fill those roles, then it makes sense to bring people in to do the work.” But I’d want to make sure it’s done right. I’d push for rules that ensure jobs are offered to locals first and that anyone coming in gets paid a fair wage—not something that undercuts the people already working here. I’d also want to see strict enforcement of labor laws to prevent exploitation.

Setting numerical limits makes sense to me too because it recognizes that there are real limits to what our country can support. I’d say, “You’ve got to have a system with some checks and balances. Otherwise, how do you plan for things like housing, schools, or healthcare?” I’d want these limits to be flexible, though—adjustable based on things like job demands, the state of the economy, and humanitarian needs. It shouldn’t be a one-size-fits-all number, but it should be a number that reflects what’s realistic and sustainable.

The policy I’d favor would probably be a combination of admitting people based on job demand and setting numerical limits. I’d also want to make sure there’s a process to prioritize people in real need—like refugees fleeing war or persecution—because even though practicality is important, you can’t ignore the human side of things. I’d say, “If we’re going to offer people a chance to come here, let’s make sure they’re ready to contribute and that we’re ready to give them a fair shot at success. But let’s not bite off more than we can chew, either.”

To me, fairness means making sure that immigration doesn’t come at the expense of the people already here, while also recognizing the value and contributions that immigrants can bring to the table. I’d focus on policies that encourage social integration—things like language classes, job training programs, and community-building efforts—so that newcomers can really become part of the fabric of the country. I’d probably sum it up by saying, “We can be welcoming without being reckless, and we can be fair without turning our backs on the people who’ve been here all along. That’s the kind of balance we need.”

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character12_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character12_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
J: You’re welcome—it’s been a meaningful experience to step into Character12_M’s shoes and share his perspective. I think what stood out most to me is how deeply his views were shaped by his background, his working-class roots, and his life experiences. He had this way of looking at things that was grounded in fairness and practicality, but also in a sense of duty to his community. It reminded me that issues like immigration aren’t just about politics; they’re about real people’s lives and how they feel those lives are being impacted.

One insight I gained is how much Character12_M’s sense of fairness extended in all directions. He was someone who believed in hard work and personal responsibility, but he also had a lot of empathy for people who were struggling. Whether it was locals who felt left behind or immigrants trying to build a better life, he wanted both groups to have a fair chance. That sense of balance feels more important than ever in today’s conversations about immigration. It’s easy to get caught up in polarizing debates, but stepping into his mindset reminded me how much we need grounded, compassionate voices like his.

This exercise also deepened my understanding of how he processed change. Character12_M wasn’t against change; he just wanted it to happen in a way that didn’t leave anyone behind or make people feel like strangers in their own communities. That’s a perspective that resonates with me now more than ever—it’s not about resisting change, but about managing it responsibly so it strengthens the sense of belonging for everyone.

As for my own views on immigration policy, this conversation has reinforced the importance of taking a balanced, pragmatic approach. It’s made me reflect on how policies need to consider both the opportunities that immigration brings and the challenges it can pose, especially for people who are already struggling. I think it’s also reminded me of the importance of dialogue—bringing people together to share their concerns, their hopes, and their ideas, just like we’ve been doing here.

Overall, embodying Character12_M has been a way to reconnect with his wisdom and his way of looking at the world. It’s reminded me of the value of listening to the perspectives of people like him—people whose voices are often overlooked but who have so much to say about what fairness, belonging, and community really mean. It’s been a privilege to carry his voice forward in this conversation, and I feel like I’ve learned from him all over again. Thank you for giving me that opportunity.
